panels.rationale: Chest CT from an article focused on hepatopulmonary syndrome shows the captioned Type 1 pulmonary vascular abnormality, matching the HPS CT finding of dilated basal pulmonary vessels. The caption specifically describes dilated peripheral arteries in the lower lobes, and the article title provides the disease attribution.
panels.attribution_text: Folador et al. Hepatopulmonary syndrome has low prevalence of pulmonary vascular abnormalities on chest computed tomography.. PloS one 2019. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0223805. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Type 1 pulmonary vascular abnormality. Type 1 pulmonary vascular abnormality was defined as the presence of dilated peripheral arteries that do not taper normally and that touch the pleural surface in the lower lobes (arrows).
in_text_mentions: The presence of pulmonary vascular abnormalities, defined as Type 1 or Type 2, was evaluated at lung window (W: 1500 HU, L: -500 HU). Type 1 abnormality (Fig 1) was defined as the presence of dilated peripheral arteries that do not taper normally and that touch the pleural surface in the lower lobes. Type 2 abnormality (Fig 2) was characterized by the presence of individual arteriovenous malformations and nodular dilatation of peripheral pulmonary vessels [12].

panels.rationale: Microbubble-contrasted echocardiography from the apical four-chamber view demonstrates delayed left ventricular opacification after five cardiac beats from right ventricular contrast enhancement, consistent with the intrapulmonary arteriovenous shunt of hepatopulmonary syndrome.

panels.figure_caption: Microbubble-contrasted echocardiography from the apical four-chamber view showed opacifications (arrows) in the left ventricle after five beats from entering the right ventricle.
in_text_mentions: the beginning to 88% at the end without oxygen supply. In addition, we found a decrease in SpO2 in the upright position (96% in the supine position to 91% in the upright position). Microbubble contrast echocardiography (CE) was performed to confirm the intrapulmonary arteriovenous shunt. We found opacifications in the left ventricle at a five-cardiac cycle delay from opacification of the right ventricle (Figure 3). A technetium-99m macroaggregated albumin (TcMAA) examination also showed 10.3% of a shunt fraction and no evidence of defects of lung perfusion and lung thromboembolism (Figure 4).

in_text_mentions: y for carbon monoxide (DLCO), measured at 48% of the predicted value. Arterial blood gas analysis highlighted an increased alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient (A-a gradient), with values of 57 mmHg in the supine position and 64 mmHg when upright. The presence of orthodeoxia coupled with the low DLCO raised clinical suspicion for HPS. To confirm the diagnosis, contrast-enhanced echocardiography was conducted. This imaging modality revealed the appearance of microbubbles in the left heart chambers starting from the fourth cardiac cycle, indicative of intrapulmonary vascular dilatations (Figure 1).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Axial contrast CT angiography of an 8-month-old infant with biliary atresia and clinically suspected hepatopulmonary syndrome; shows diffuse dilatation of the pulmonary vasculature, the CT hallmark of intrapulmonary vascular dilatation in HPS. B: Caudal section of the same CT angiography showing prominent dilated basal pulmonary vessels, consistent with hepatopulmonary syndrome vasculopathy. C: Most caudal CT section demonstrating the most prominent dilatation of the basal pulmonary vasculature in a patient with hepatopulmonary syndrome.

in_text_mentions: vidence of hepatic dysfunction or hyperammonemia was identified at presentation. In view of cyanosis and recurrent respiratory symptoms, a detailed cardiopulmonary evaluation was undertaken. Two-dimensional echocardiography revealed no structural cardiac abnormality or intracardiac shunt. Subsequently, contrast-enhanced CT pulmonary angiography was performed, which demonstrated marked dilatation of segmental and subsegmental pulmonary vessels with diffuse peripheral vascular prominence, findings consistent with hepatopulmonary syndrome secondary to an underlying portosystemic shunt (Figure 1).

panels.rationale: Single-panel contrast-enhanced echocardiogram from a patient with hepatopulmonary syndrome; chamber labels (LV, RV, LA, RA) and ECG trace are overlaid. The caption describes microbubbles reaching the left atrium 6 cardiac cycles after the right atrium, the hallmark delayed intrapulmonary shunt pattern that confirms HPS, matching the vocabulary finding hepatopulmonary_syndrome_intrapulmonary_arteriovenous_shunt. Real patient echocardiographic image, no third-party copyright indication.

in_text_mentions: appeared in the right atrium suggests the presence of a PFO. However, if this material arrives to the left atrium after 4–8 cardiac cycles prove the presence of dilate pulmonary microvasculature confirming the diagnosis of HPS. In our patient Contrast-enhanced echocardiography showed the presence of a PFO (Figure 1) and the arrival of contrast material to the right atrium 6 cardiac cycles after it was first seen in the left atrium (Figure 2). Existence of this PFO poses a diagnostic challenge since structural heart diseases must be excluded before HPS can be diagnose with certainty [2, 15–17].
